local.levelRationale: Anchor: 61.8% of New Yorkers (5.04M of 8.16M) fall below the City's own True Cost of Living threshold, against an implied target of 0% — the threshold is by definition the income needed to be independent of public and private assistance, and Charter Amendment 3 (Nov 2022, 81% approval) mandates the City to measure and report it annually. 13% of residents (~1M people) are below even HALF the threshold, and government transfers close only ~5 percentage points of the gap (67% pre-transfer to 62% post). An independent measure on a different methodology agrees on the order of magnitude: FCNY's Self-Sufficiency Standard puts 46% of working-age households below its threshold on 2024 incomes. R1 upward adjustments: Poverty Tracker at a record 26% in 2024 (2.2M people, twice the national rate); 2024 Gini of 0.5563, now second-highest among large US cities (up from 4th); Bronx good-job rate of 20% vs 46% in Manhattan; Black unemployment 8.9% (Dec 2025), over 3x white, with young Black workers at 23.8% (2024); and a 66-point neighborhood spread on the TCOL measure itself (80% in Mott Haven/Hunts Point to 14% in the Financial District). R1 downward adjustments, weighed and named: the FCNY series shows inadequacy falling from its 2021 peak (though still above pre-pandemic, and RISING for single-full-time-earner households, 40%→44%); citywide unemployment a moderate 5.2% (2025 annual average); real median household income up 2.2% in 2024; and the strongest actively-enforced municipal labour-standards regime in the country ($17 minimum wage, $22.13 delivery-worker floor upheld twice in federal court in Jan 2026, Fair Workweek with $8.5M recovered since Jan 2026, statewide Freelance Isn't Free). Those are why this is 100 rather than 130 or 150 — they are policy responses and a moderating trend, not evidence that a majority of the city can currently cover basic needs — and they do not support anything below 100. Caveat capping confidence rather than level: the headline is 2022-vintage data published in 2026.
local.indicator: NYC True Cost of Living (TCOL) Measure — share of residents below the true cost of living threshold
local.value: 61.8% of New Yorkers (5.04M of 8.16M residents) below the TCOL threshold citywide, measured AFTER government supports; 67% before supports, i.e. transfers close ~5 percentage points. Universe is persons in families, all ages. A further 3.58M New Yorkers are above the federal poverty line but still below the TCOL threshold (the 'missing middle'), and 13% of residents (~1M people) are below HALF the threshold. Families with children face a median cost of $159,197/yr against median resources of $124,007 (78% of cost), an average gap of $35,190 — of which market resources supply $95,277 and government transfers $28,730. Citywide, persons in families below the threshold have an average annual resource gap of $39,603 (median costs $122,919 vs median resources $78,993). 73% of NYC children (1.2M) live in families below the threshold, rising to 86.8% in the Bronx. The highest rate of any group: 92% of people in families with a self-care disability (working-age adults under 65), with an average gap of $76,178; the broader any-disability rates are 80.3% (under 65) and 68.1% (65+).
local.target: The TCOL threshold is itself the benchmark: implied target 0% of residents below it. Charter Amendment 3 (November 2022, approved by 81% of voters — the third of three racial justice ballot measures) mandates the City to create and annually report a measure of what it actually costs to live in New York City, and the measure defines the threshold as 'the resources necessary for individuals and families to be independent of public and private assistance.' The report itself states no numeric reduction target. Independent cross-check: FCNY/United Way/Center for Women's Welfare Self-Sufficiency Standard, 46% of working-age households below its threshold (2024 incomes, 2026 costs). Secondary equity benchmark: MOERJ's Preliminary Citywide Racial Equity Plan goal of closing racial TCOL gaps (Hispanic 77.6%, Black 65.6%, Asian/Pacific Islander 63.3%, White 43.7%).
local.context: A purpose-built official city measure rather than a federal proxy, mandated by Charter Amendment 3 (Nov 2022) and published in its inaugural edition by MOERJ with the Mayor's Office for Economic Opportunity and the Urban Institute — report dated March 2026, released April 6, 2026 as part of the Mamdani administration's first-100-days package. VINTAGE CAVEAT (important): all estimates come from the Urban Institute's ATTIS model applied to 2018 American Community Survey data projected to 2022, so this is a 2022-vintage estimate published in 2026, with a population base of 8.16M residents. The measure adapts the Urban Institute's True Cost of Economic Security framework and, unlike the NYCgov poverty measure, asks what it takes to be independent of assistance rather than whether a poverty threshold is met — the report is explicit that the two are complementary rather than directly comparable. The threshold includes housing, food, health care, child care, transportation, taxes, a savings target set at 10% of expenses, and other necessities. RECONCILIATION with the other 'True Cost of Living' series (per R11): FCNY/United Way's NYC True Cost of Living reports 46% of WORKING-AGE HOUSEHOLDS below threshold (2024 ACS 1-year PUMS, incomes adjusted to 2026 costs), and 50% in its 2023 report (1,298,212 households, 2,991,973 people) against 36% in 2021. The 16-point gap to 62% is not a discrepancy but four definitional differences: unit (persons vs households), universe (all residents vs working-age households, FCNY explicitly excluding adults 65+, group quarters, and adults with work-limiting disabilities — precisely MOERJ's highest-rate groups), threshold basket (savings target included vs Self-Sufficiency Standard with none), and vintage (2022 vs 2024/2026). Note the direction check: FCNY measures resources BEFORE any assistance and still lands lower than MOERJ's post-transfer figure, confirming transfers are not the driver of the gap. TREND: the FCNY series is the only one with a real time trend and it declined 2012-2019, rose sharply in 2021, and declined again by 2024 — still 'substantially higher than pre-pandemic levels, despite declining from the 2021 peak.' FCNY attributes the decline to composition rather than easing affordability: fewer no-worker households as the labour market recovered, and a 1.2pp fall in the share of households with children (who face higher thresholds). Critically, inadequacy among households with one full-time year-round worker ROSE from 40% (2021) to 44% (2024), and rose among all working households — full-time work is increasingly insufficient. The scale dwarfs a small city like Petaluma: a majority of an 8.2M-person city cannot cover basic needs while working, and the Hispanic-white gap (77.6% vs 43.7%) is itself wider than the entire gap between Petaluma's poverty rate and the US average. Policy levers: MOERJ's Preliminary Citywide Racial Equity Plan (45 agencies, 200+ goals, 800+ strategies) and the Council's '30 For Our City' minimum-wage bill.
local.source: NYC Mayor's Office of Equity & Racial Justice (MOERJ), with the Mayor's Office for Economic Opportunity and the Urban Institute — 'NYC True Cost of Living Measure: Inaugural Report' (dated March 2026, released April 6, 2026); Urban Institute companion report 'Bridging the True Cost of Living Gap in New York City' (Acs, Dehry, Simpson & Todd, May 14, 2026)
local.boroughLevelNote: Borough TCOL rates are genuinely published at borough level in the primary report (Table 9, p.43; Table 10, p.44), sourced 'Urban Institute, ATTIS model, 2022. MOERJ compilation from borough-level data', and independently corroborated by the Urban Institute companion report. None is interpolated or pro-rated. Levels are monotone in the borough TCOL rate and consistent with the citywide 100; values off the scale anchors (130, 70) are interpolated between anchors, as R1's worked example permits.

bronx.value: 75.1% below the TCOL threshold — highest of the five boroughs and 13.3 points above citywide; 86.8% of persons in families with children; 15.6% below half the threshold (highest deep-hardship rate in the city); average resource gap $39,692. The report notes the Bronx has the lowest costs of any borough but also the least resources.
bronx.levelNote: 130 is interpolated between critical (100) and severe (150): pushed above the citywide 100 by the citywide-highest TCOL rate, the 86.8% child rate, the highest deep-hardship rate (15.6%), the highest borough unemployment (6.8%, 2025 annual average) and the lowest good-job rate (~20%).
bronx.source: NYC MOERJ, 'NYC True Cost of Living Measure: Inaugural Report' (Tables 9-10)

brooklyn.value: 61.5% below the TCOL threshold — at the citywide average; 73.1% of persons in families with children; average resource gap $38,208; Hispanic 75.1%, Black 64.8%, Asian/PI 64.7%, White 50.3%
brooklyn.source: NYC MOERJ, 'NYC True Cost of Living Measure: Inaugural Report' (Tables 9-10)

manhattan.value: 55.6% below the TCOL threshold — below the citywide 61.8% — but the widest racial gap of any borough: Hispanic 85.3%, Black 79.7%, Asian/PI 54.5%, White 32.9%, a 52-point Hispanic-white spread against 35 points in the Bronx. Also the highest average resource gap of any borough ($44,529) and the second-highest deep-hardship rate in the city (15.2% below half the threshold), reflecting economic polarization; 57.8% of persons in families with children.
manhattan.levelNote: Held at the citywide 100 rather than softened to 90 per R1: the headline rate is below citywide, but the 15.2% deep-hardship rate, the 52-point racial gap, the largest average resource gap and the highest borough Gini (0.5944, 2024) are material well-sourced shortfalls inside the same borough.
manhattan.source: NYC MOERJ, 'NYC True Cost of Living Measure: Inaugural Report' (Tables 9-10)

queens.value: 61.1% below the TCOL threshold — at the citywide average; 71.5% of persons in families with children; average resource gap $37,953; Hispanic 71.1%, Black 56.2%, Asian/PI 65.3%, White 48.4%
queens.source: NYC MOERJ, 'NYC True Cost of Living Measure: Inaugural Report' (Tables 9-10)

statenIsland.value: 48.2% below the TCOL threshold — lowest of the five boroughs and 27 points below the Bronx, but still nearly half of residents; 57.1% of persons in families with children; lowest deep-hardship rate in the city (9.0%); average resource gap $39,861; Hispanic 63.9%, Black 62.8%, Asian/PI 55.2%, White 39.6%
statenIsland.levelNote: 70 is interpolated between 'needs attention' (50) and 'critical' (100), reflecting a rate below the citywide average and the city's lowest deep-hardship rate and lowest Gini (0.4374, 2024), against a still-severe absolute level of nearly half of residents below threshold.
statenIsland.source: NYC MOERJ, 'NYC True Cost of Living Measure: Inaugural Report' (Tables 9-10)

local.neighborhoodNote: The sharpest disaggregation available is on the dimension's own indicator rather than a proxy: FCNY's 'Overlooked & Undercounted in New York City 2026' reports the share of households below the True Cost of Living ranging from 80% in Bronx Community Districts 1 & 2 (Melrose, Mott Haven, Longwood, Hunts Point) to 14% in Manhattan Community Districts 1 & 2 (Financial District, Greenwich Village) — a 66-point spread, and arguably the single sharpest income-and-work disparity in the portrait. The same brief finds 86% of single mothers with young children below the threshold, and notes that 40% of households have at least one child in Bronx CDs 1 & 2 versus 19% in Manhattan CDs 1 & 2. Federal-poverty contrast, from the 2024 ACS: citywide 18.0%, Bronx 28.8%, Brooklyn 19.2%, Manhattan 15.6%, Queens 13.3%, Staten Island 11.1% — the Bronx remains the poorest large urban county in the nation on conventional measures.

subIndicators.name: FCNY/United Way NYC True Cost of Living (independent co-measure, Self-Sufficiency Standard)
subIndicators.value: 46% of working-age NYC households below the True Cost of Living (15% below the Official Poverty Measure plus a further 31% above poverty but still short of basic needs); 50% in the 2023 report (1,298,212 households, 2,991,973 people) and 36% in the 2021 report. Universe excludes adults 65+, group quarters and adults with work-limiting disabilities; measured with NO public or private assistance counted. Trend: declined 2012-2019, rose sharply in 2021, declined again by 2024, but remains substantially above pre-pandemic — and inadequacy among households with one full-time year-round worker ROSE from 40% (2021) to 44% (2024).
subIndicators.source: Center for Women's Welfare, University of Washington School of Social Work, for the Fund for the City of New York / United Way of NYC — 'Overlooked & Undercounted in New York City 2026' (March 18, 2026); 2024 ACS 1-year PUMS with incomes adjusted to 2026 cost benchmarks
subIndicators.note: Not interchangeable with the 61.8% MOERJ headline — different unit, universe, basket and vintage. See local.context for the full reconciliation.

subIndicators.name: Poverty Tracker (independent, Columbia University / Robin Hood Foundation)
subIndicators.value: 26% overall poverty rate in 2024 — twice the national rate and the highest since the Poverty Tracker began — affecting 2.2M people (1.7M adults, nearly 450,000 children); nearly 5 million New Yorkers, 3 in 5, live below 200% of the poverty line
subIndicators.source: Robin Hood / Columbia University Center on Poverty and Social Policy, 'The State of Poverty and Disadvantage in New York City' Vol. 8 (released March 2026)
subIndicators.note: Vol. 7 (Feb 2025) reported 25% on 2023 data, 2.02M people — cite the correct volume when quoting.

subIndicators.name: Federal/ACS poverty rate (contrast measure)
subIndicators.value: 18.0% of persons at or below the federal poverty line citywide (2024 ACS), down 0.2pp from 2023 and 5.9 points above the US rate of 12.1%; by borough Bronx 28.8%, Brooklyn 19.2%, Manhattan 15.6%, Queens 13.3%, Staten Island 11.1%; by age under-18 24.2%, 18-64 15.4%, 65+ 20.2%. Race/ethnicity breakdown available only for 2023: Hispanic 24.8%, Black 21.7%, Asian 16.8%, White 11.5%.
subIndicators.source: U.S. Census Bureau 2024 ACS as compiled in NYC Rent Guidelines Board, '2026 Income and Affordability Study' (April 16, 2026); 2023 race breakdown from Community Service Society of NY analysis of ACS

subIndicators.name: Gini index of income inequality (ACS B19083)
subIndicators.value: 0.5563 citywide (2024), up from 0.5546 in 2023 — the second-highest among large U.S. cities, behind only Miami (0.5637), against a U.S. coefficient of 0.4809; by borough Manhattan 0.5944, Brooklyn 0.5347, Bronx 0.5336, Queens 0.4694, Staten Island 0.4374
subIndicators.source: NYC Rent Guidelines Board, '2026 Income and Affordability Study' (April 16, 2026), ACS B19083 vintage 2024

subIndicators.name: Median household income
subIndicators.value: $81,228 citywide (2024 ACS), up 6.1% nominally and 2.2% in real terms vs 2023; renter households $64,866 (+1.8% real), owner households $121,443 (-0.4% real). Renter income by borough rose most in Staten Island (+36.2% real) and Manhattan (+6.9%), and fell in the Bronx.
subIndicators.source: U.S. Census Bureau 2024 ACS as compiled in NYC Rent Guidelines Board, '2026 Income and Affordability Study'
subIndicators.note: Supersedes an earlier Furman-attributed citywide figure of $83,970 that could not be reconciled with the published 2024 ACS value; per R3 the published figure is used. A clean single-vintage five-borough median-household-income set was not assembled — the borough detail here is renter-income change, not level.

subIndicators.name: 'Good job' rate by borough (living wage + full-time year-round + employer health insurance + safe conditions)
subIndicators.value: Citywide 33.2%; Manhattan ~46%, Staten Island ~37%, Brooklyn ~33%, Queens ~28%, Bronx ~20%. A job counts only if it pays a living wage for the worker's household size, is 35+ hrs/week and 50+ weeks/year, carries employer-sponsored health insurance, and is either safe or pays a 25% hazard premium.
subIndicators.source: Office of the NYC Comptroller (Brad Lander), 'The State of Job Quality in New York City' (published May 14, 2025; 2017-2023 series). Mark Levine is the current Comptroller but did not issue this report.

subIndicators.name: Unemployment rate by race/ethnicity
subIndicators.value: Black 8.9%, Hispanic 6.3%, Asian 3.5%, White under 3% (December 2025) — the Black rate over 3x the white rate. Against December 2019: Hispanic was 4.9% (now 1.4 points higher) and Asian 1.8% (now 1.7 points higher); white unemployment is closest to pre-pandemic.
subIndicators.source: NY State Comptroller DiNapoli, 'Post-Pandemic Unemployment in NYC Persists for Some Demographic Groups' (April 7, 2026 release, December 2025 data)

subIndicators.name: Youth unemployment
subIndicators.value: Young Black workers at 23.8% unemployment in 2024, nine points above 2019; overall 16-24 youth unemployment 13.2% in 2024, 3.6 points above 2019, with Black, Hispanic and Asian youth — especially young men — above the overall youth rate
subIndicators.source: NY State Comptroller DiNapoli, 'Youth in NYC Face Double-Digit Unemployment Rate' (June 2025)

subIndicators.name: Unemployment rate by borough
subIndicators.value: Citywide annual average 5.2% in 2025, up 0.2pp from 5.0% in 2024 and 1.2 points above 2019; by borough Bronx 6.8% (consistently highest), Brooklyn 5.2%, Queens 4.6%, Manhattan 4.6%, Staten Island 4.5% (lowest). Rates fell 0.1-0.2pp in every borough. Latest month available: January 2026 at 5.5% citywide, 0.7pp above January 2025.
subIndicators.source: BLS / NYS Dept. of Labor Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), as published in NYC Rent Guidelines Board '2026 Income and Affordability Study' (April 16, 2026)
subIndicators.note: Single-vintage official five-borough set; supersedes an earlier mixed-vintage third-party (FRED/Trading Economics) assembly whose Queens, Staten Island and Manhattan values were incorrect.

subIndicators.name: NY minimum wage in NYC
subIndicators.value: $17.00/hr effective Jan 1, 2026 (up from $16.50 in 2025) in NYC, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester; $16.00 in the rest of the state. Tipped food service workers $11.35 cash wage with a $5.65 tip credit; other tipped service employees $14.15 with a $2.85 credit. The statutory $0.50 step schedule ends with 2026; from 2027 the wage is indexed annually to CPI-W for the Northeast region.
subIndicators.source: NYS Department of Labor / Gov. Hochul minimum wage schedule (2023 state law)

subIndicators.name: App-based delivery worker minimum pay rate
subIndicators.value: $22.13/hr as of April 1, 2026, up from $21.44 — a 3.2% inflation adjustment for Dec 2024-Dec 2025 — covering both food and third-party grocery delivery workers; first-in-the-nation standard. Enforcement has produced a $5,195,000 settlement with Uber Eats, Fantuan and HungryPanda covering more than 49,000 workers (Uber Eats $3.15M restitution to 48,000+ plus $350K penalties for unpaid canceled-trip time Dec 2023-Sep 2024; HungryPanda $1,068,672 to 1,000+; Fantuan $468K+ to 285), plus Uber's agreement to reinstate as many as 10,000 wrongfully deactivated workers. DCWP is separately suing non-compliant platforms, having found Motoclick workers earning $3.67-$4.67/hr.
subIndicators.source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP)

subIndicators.name: Average Wall Street bonus vs. typical wage
subIndicators.value: $246,900 average bonus for 2025, up 6%, on a record $49.2B bonus pool; average total securities-industry compensation $505,677 in 2024, up 7.3% and the second-highest on record — roughly 5x the average private-sector salary elsewhere in the city. The securities sector accounted for 20.2% of all NYC economic activity in 2024, 8.4% of city tax revenue in City FY2025 and 19.4% of state tax collections in SFY2024-25, while 1 in 13 city jobs is directly or indirectly tied to it.
subIndicators.source: NY State Comptroller DiNapoli, Wall Street bonus report (March 2026)

subIndicators.name: Freelance/gig workforce share
subIndicators.value: ~1.3 million people, ~34% of NYC's workforce, performed freelance work in the prior 12 months, generating an estimated $31.4B in annual earnings; 29% freelanced full-time, 50% part-time, 20% as supplemental income
subIndicators.source: Freelancers Union and Upwork with the NYC Mayor's Office of Media and Entertainment, 'Freelancing in New York City' (September 2019)
subIndicators.note: Pre-pandemic and seven years stale — the only comprehensive city-scale freelance estimate located. Treat as indicative only; no post-2019 update was found.

subIndicators.name: Childcare cost as labor-force barrier
subIndicators.value: Roughly 375,000 city parents left a job or reduced work commitments in 2022 due to inadequate child care access, at an estimated cost of $23 billion in lost economic output, $5.9 billion in lost disposable income and $2.2 billion in lost tax revenue. Quality care is unaffordable for 80% of NY families, at an average $26,000 per child annually and up to $40,000.
subIndicators.source: Citizens' Committee for Children of New York (CCC), 'NYC Needs Universal Child Care'

global.levelRationale: Two quantified transmission channels running outward from NYC, both worsening on the labour-and-capital side and only partially offset on the civic side. Capital allocation: JPMorgan Chase, headquartered in NYC, is the world's single largest fossil-fuel financier at $58B in 2025 (up 12.6%), with fellow NYC-headquartered Citigroup in the global top five at $45-47B; financing to companies actively EXPANDING fossil fuels surged 27% to $508B in 2025, the Net-Zero Banking Alliance collapsed, and JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs abandoned their coal and Arctic exclusions outright. Labour: roughly 412,000 undocumented New Yorkers remain excluded from unemployment insurance and much baseline labour-law protection, concentrated in the delivery, domestic-work, food-service and construction sectors that underpin the city's consumption, with no permanent successor to the lapsed 2021 Excluded Workers Fund. Offsetting, and real: NYC's own public pension funds run one of the most prominent divestment programmes in U.S. public finance, which survived final appellate review in October 2025 and beat its 2025 interim emissions target a year early (37% reduction 2019-2024). That contradiction between the city's private financial sector and its public capital is the finding, and it is critical-tier because the private side is the larger and growing quantity. Confidence is capped at medium because the remittance channel — the most on-dimension global-social flow for income & work — remains unquantified.
global.indicator: NYC's outward income-and-work footprint: workers excluded from labour protection inside the city, and NYC-headquartered banks' fossil-fuel capital allocation set against NYC public pension divestment
global.value: LABOUR CHANNEL: An estimated ~412,000 undocumented New Yorkers (NYC Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs, 2022; down from ~611,000 in 2012; NYC Comptroller estimated ~476,000 in 2019) are excluded from unemployment insurance and many labour protections, and are disproportionately exposed to wage theft. New York State's 2021 Excluded Workers Fund distributed more than $2B of its $2.1B appropriation to more than 130,000 approved applicants — 99% receiving the Tier 1 benefit of $15,600 — before exhausting by December 2021, with no permanent successor enacted as of mid-2026. CAPITAL CHANNEL: JPMorgan Chase (HQ: NYC) financed $58B in fossil fuels in 2025, up 12.6% and the largest of any bank in the world; Citigroup (HQ: NYC) is in the global top five at roughly $45-47B. Of the 2025 top five, only JPMorgan and Citigroup are NYC-headquartered — Bank of America ($47B) is Charlotte, MUFG ($47B) and Mizuho are Tokyo. The world's 65 largest banks financed fossil fuels with $906B in 2025 (+8% year-over-year) and $8.7 trillion since the 2016 Paris Agreement, with financing to fossil-fuel expanders up 27% to $508B. CIVIC COUNTERWEIGHT: three of NYC's five public pension systems (Teachers' Retirement System, NYCERS, Board of Education Retirement System) voted to divest from publicly-traded fossil-fuel reserve owners in 2021 and completed divestment in 2022, added an upstream private-markets exclusion in 2023, and hold a 2040 net-zero portfolio target with a $50B climate-solutions goal by 2035; weighted-average financed Scope 1+2 emissions fell 37% between 2019 and 2024, beating the 2025 interim targets a year early. Litigation challenging the divestment (Wong et al. v. NYCERS) was dismissed for lack of standing, affirmed on appeal, and the New York Court of Appeals denied leave to appeal on October 21, 2025 — final. Divestment has NOT been reversed.
global.target: No binding target exists for NYC-headquartered banks' financed emissions — this is private-sector activity outside city jurisdiction. The closest civic-side commitments are the NYC pension funds' 2040 net-zero portfolio target and $50B-by-2035 climate-solutions goal (NYC Comptroller / Bureau of Asset Management). On the labour side, the aspirational benchmark is universal coverage: the proposed Unemployment Bridge Program (NY Senate Bill S173, 2025) as a permanent successor to the Excluded Workers Fund, which would extend unemployment-style support to excluded and undocumented workers.
global.context: NYC's global-social footprint in income & work runs through two channels. The labour channel is the on-dimension one: roughly 412,000 undocumented residents form part of an informal economy underpinning low-wage sectors that make the city's consumption possible, while remaining outside unemployment insurance and disproportionately exposed to wage theft — a transmission that also runs outward through the households and countries those workers support. The capital channel is the quantified one: the same city that hosts the world's largest fossil-fuel underwriter also manages, through its Comptroller-run pension funds, one of the most prominent divestment programmes in U.S. public finance, transmitted through securities underwriting and lending and through shareholder-engagement campaigns the Comptroller runs on banks the city does business with. Both are distinctly big-city phenomena with no Petaluma equivalent. CROSS-DIMENSION WARNING: the fossil-finance material is a climate transmission channel as much as an income-and-work one and is likely to appear in the climate change dimension's global lens; the orchestrator should decide where it lives to avoid double-counting. DATA GAPS: no credible NYC-specific dollar estimate for remittances sent abroad from the city could be located, which is the most obviously on-dimension global-social flow for this dimension and is flagged rather than estimated. Two live pension-policy statuses could not be confirmed and are stated as unresolved rather than asserted: whether trustees adopted the December 2024 proposal to exclude future private-market midstream/downstream fossil-fuel investment, and the outcome of the June 30, 2025 deadline for public-markets asset managers to file compliant net-zero plans.
global.source: Oil Change International / Rainforest Action Network et al., 'Banking on Climate Chaos 2026' (published June 8, 2026, covering 2025 data); NYC Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs; NYC Comptroller's Office; NYS Department of Labor; NY State Senate

policyAnchors.name: NYC True Cost of Living Measure & Preliminary Citywide Racial Equity Plan (2026)
policyAnchors.relevance: First official city-government TCOL measure and racial equity plan for income/work outcomes, mandated by Charter Amendment 3 of November 2022 (approved by 81% of voters, the third of three racial justice ballot measures); sets the baseline (61.8% below TCOL) used as this dimension's headline indicator, and the Charter requires annual reporting.
policyAnchors.status2026: Inaugural report dated March 2026, released April 6, 2026 by the Mamdani administration (Mayor's Office of Equity & Racial Justice under Chief Equity Officer and Commissioner Afua Atta-Mensah, appointed January 2026, with the Mayor's Office for Economic Opportunity and the Urban Institute). The Racial Equity Plan is explicitly 'preliminary', with 45 agencies, 200+ goals and 800+ strategies still being finalized. Data vintage is 2022 (2018 ACS projected forward via the Urban Institute ATTIS model), so the next release should be watched for a genuine update.

policyAnchors.name: '30 For Our City' minimum wage bill (NYC Council)
policyAnchors.relevance: Would raise the NYC minimum wage well beyond the state-set floor — to $20/hr by 2027 and $30/hr by 2030 for employers with more than 500 employees, and $30/hr by 2032 for smaller employers. Would be the highest municipal minimum wage in the United States.
policyAnchors.status2026: Introduced by Council Member Sandy Nurse and announced March 10, 2026 under the 'Raise Up NY' banner, publicly backed by Mayor Mamdani and a bloc of Council members; under consideration in the Council with no full-Council vote as of late July 2026. Committee assignment not independently confirmed.

policyAnchors.name: NY State minimum wage schedule (2023 state law)
policyAnchors.relevance: Sets the current wage floor for NYC and the indexing mechanism beyond 2026.
policyAnchors.status2026: In effect: $17.00/hr in NYC, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester as of Jan 1, 2026; $16.00 in the rest of the state. State law schedules the last flat $0.50 step for 2026, then CPI-W (Northeast region) indexed annual increases beginning 2027.

policyAnchors.name: App-Based Delivery Workers' Minimum Pay Rate (NYC Local Law / DCWP rule, 2021-23, amended 2025-26)
policyAnchors.relevance: First-in-the-nation minimum pay standard for app-based food and grocery delivery workers.
policyAnchors.status2026: In effect and actively enforced; rate rose to $22.13/hr on April 1, 2026. Amended rules took effect January 26, 2026, extending minimum pay to grocery delivery workers, requiring up-front tipping options, written pay statements within seven days, and trip-distance disclosure. Industry challenges failed on both fronts in SDNY on or about January 22, 2026: Judge John Koeltl denied a preliminary injunction against the grocery-delivery minimum pay requirements and subsequently denied an injunction pending appeal, while Judge George Daniels denied injunctive relief against the up-front tipping framework, which platforms challenged as compelled speech. A request to stay proceedings pending appeal was still being adjudicated. DCWP has extracted a $5,195,000 settlement from Uber Eats, Fantuan and HungryPanda covering 49,000+ workers plus reinstatement of up to 10,000 deactivated workers, and is suing non-compliant platforms.

policyAnchors.name: NYC Fair Workweek Law (Local Laws 66-69 of 2017)
policyAnchors.relevance: Predictive-scheduling and just-cause protections for fast-food and retail workers, a major lever against income volatility for low-wage NYC workers.
policyAnchors.status2026: Actively enforced by DCWP under the Mamdani administration; more than $8.5M in restitution recovered since Jan 1, 2026, including a settlement of over $1.5M affecting 760+ workers (March 2026) and an action against a premium retailer (Theory LLC, ~$277K).

policyAnchors.name: Earned Safe and Sick Time Act (ESSTA) expansion
policyAnchors.relevance: Expands paid/unpaid safe-and-sick leave categories relevant to low-wage and gig-adjacent workers' income stability.
policyAnchors.status2026: Expanded provisions took effect Feb 22, 2026, adding up to 32 hours of frontloaded unpaid safe/sick leave atop existing paid leave (40-56 hrs depending on employer size), and new usable categories including housing court proceedings, workplace-violence recovery and disaster response.

policyAnchors.name: Freelance Isn't Free Act
policyAnchors.relevance: Protects freelance workers — roughly a third of the NYC workforce on the last comprehensive count — from nonpayment.
policyAnchors.status2026: NYC's 2016 local law was extended statewide effective Aug 28, 2024 (NY General Business Law Article 44-A); in effect, enforced by NYS DOL and NYC DCWP.

policyAnchors.name: City of Yes for Economic Opportunity
policyAnchors.relevance: Citywide zoning reform intended to expand job-creating business types and reduce regulatory barriers to work.
policyAnchors.status2026: Adopted by City Council June 6, 2024 under the Adams administration; zoning changes are permanent and remain in effect under the Mamdani administration, with continuing implementation (industrial strategic plan, enforcement resourcing commitments).

policyAnchors.name: Excluded Workers Fund (2021) / proposed Unemployment Bridge Program
policyAnchors.relevance: Precedent for extending unemployment-style support to undocumented and other excluded workers; its lapse is the central unresolved gap in labour protection for NYC's excluded workforce.
policyAnchors.status2026: The 2021 New York State fund appropriated $2.1B and distributed more than $2B to more than 130,000 approved applicants — 99% at the Tier 1 benefit of $15,600 — before exhausting by December 2021, and was never replaced. A permanent successor, the Unemployment Bridge Program (NY Senate Bill S173, 2025, proposed to be funded by a digital-advertising tax on large tech firms), had not been enacted as of mid-2026.

policyAnchors.name: NYC public pension fossil-fuel divestment and 2040 net-zero commitment
policyAnchors.relevance: The city's own capital is the one part of the finance channel NYC government directly controls; it is the counterweight to NYC-headquartered private banks' fossil-fuel financing in the global lens.
policyAnchors.status2026: In force and judicially settled. TRS, NYCERS and BERS voted to divest from publicly-traded fossil-fuel reserve owners in 2021 and completed divestment in 2022; an upstream private-markets exclusion was added in 2023; the 2040 net-zero portfolio target and a $50B-by-2035 climate-solutions goal stand, with weighted-average financed Scope 1+2 emissions down 37% between 2019 and 2024, beating the 2025 interim targets a year early. Wong et al. v. NYCERS was dismissed for lack of standing, affirmed on appeal, and the NY Court of Appeals denied leave to appeal on October 21, 2025 — final; divestment has not been reversed. UNRESOLVED: whether trustees adopted the December 2024 proposal to exclude future private-market midstream/downstream fossil-fuel investment, and the outcome of the June 30, 2025 asset-manager net-zero-plan deadline. Note the office has changed hands — this work is Comptroller Brad Lander's; Mark Levine is the current Comptroller.

petalumaContrast: Petaluma's own data.js lists a 6.5% poverty rate (2024, ACS) and a 0.44 Gini coefficient (2019) — figures that would represent enormous success by NYC standards. NYC's citywide Gini is 0.5563 (2024), the second-highest among large U.S. cities, with Manhattan alone at 0.5944, and 61.8% of New Yorkers fall short of the city's own True Cost of Living threshold (46% of working-age households on the independent FCNY measure) against Petaluma's much narrower affordability strain (34% cost-burdened on housing). The scale and mechanism also differ qualitatively: Petaluma has no equivalent to NYC's finance-sector wealth concentration (a $246,900 average Wall Street bonus for 2025 against Petaluma's local median incomes) or to a roughly 412,000-person undocumented workforce excluded from unemployment insurance. Note that the two portraits are NOT measuring the same thing when they both say 'poverty': Petaluma's 6.5% is the federal poverty rate, whose NYC equivalent is 18.0% (2024) — the 61.8% figure is a self-sufficiency threshold and must not be compared to it directly.
dataGaps: No NYC-specific dollar estimate for remittances sent abroad from the city could be located. This is the most on-dimension global-social flow for income & work and its absence is why the global lens leans on the finance channel. The NYC Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs (MOIA) or the Center for Migration Studies of New York (CMSNY) would be the most likely holders of city-scale remittance modeling.

The headline TCOL Measure is built on 2018 ACS data projected to 2022, published in 2026. No post-2022 vintage of the official measure exists yet, so the dimension cannot say what the official rate is today — and the independent FCNY series suggests conditions improved somewhat between 2021 and 2024. MOERJ and the Mayor's Office for Economic Opportunity should be asked for the update cadence the Charter's annual-reporting mandate implies.

The official 'NYCgov Poverty Measure' (Mayor's Office for Economic Opportunity / NYC Opportunity) publishes on a multi-year lag and no current-year percentage could be located from NYC Opportunity itself; its Poverty Research Team would have the authoritative current figure and could clarify how the NYCgov measure relates to the new TCOL measure.

No current, city-specific wage-theft dollar total was found. The widely-cited '$20 million/week' figure traces to former Manhattan DA Cyrus Vance (pre-2022) and is stale — the NYC Comptroller's Bureau of Labor Law or NYS DOL's Division of Labor Standards would hold current recovery totals.

Garment and retail global sourcing labour conditions specific to NYC-headquartered or NYC-based retailers were not quantified. NYC Economic Development Corporation (garment district initiatives) or the Worker Rights Consortium would be better positioned.

No single-vintage five-borough median household income table was assembled; the citywide 2024 ACS figure is used instead. Borough-level ACS income tables exist in the Rent Guidelines Board study appendices and should be extracted directly.

Estimates of NYC's undocumented population are ACS-modelled and range widely by method and year (~412,000 per MOIA for 2022, ~476,000 per the NYC Comptroller for 2019, ~611,000 in 2012). Note explicitly that Center for Migration Studies figures in the 600,000-670,000 range are NEW YORK STATE, not the city, and must not be substituted.

questionsForOrchestrator: The headline is 2022-vintage data (2018 ACS projected to 2022 via the Urban Institute ATTIS model) published in March/April 2026. It is unambiguously the officially mandated city measure at the right geography, so R3 argues for headlining it — but the one series with a real time trend (FCNY) shows income inadequacy falling between 2021 and 2024. Confirm the 2022-vintage official measure should stay as headline with the 2024-vintage FCNY figure as a labelled co-measure rather than the reverse.

RESOLVED for the record (R11): the 62%-vs-50% divergence is not an error. 61.8% is persons in families, all ages, 2022, post-transfer, on the Urban Institute TCES basket including a 10%-of-expenses savings target; 46-50% is working-age households only, pre-transfer, on the Self-Sufficiency Standard basket with no savings component. Should other dimensions citing an NYC 'true cost of living' or self-sufficiency figure be flagged to state which measure they mean? The two differ by 16 percentage points and are not interchangeable.

RESOLVED, correcting this dossier's own earlier question: the orchestrator's brief was right and the research agent was wrong on the undocumented population. The 600,000-670,000 and 820,400 figures are NEW YORK STATE (CMS: 672,000 statewide, 2022); the NYC figure is ~412,000 (MOIA, 2022), down from ~611,000 in 2012, with the Comptroller at ~476,000 for 2019. Any other dimension that picked up 600,000+ as a city figure needs the same correction — please sweep for it.

Cross-dimension duplication: the JPMorgan Chase / Banking on Climate Chaos material is the quantified backbone of this global-social lens, but financed emissions are a climate transmission channel and will likely anchor the climate change dimension's global lens too. Decide where it lives. If it stays here, the labour channel should lead (as it now does) with finance as the quantified co-channel; if it moves to climate, this global lens needs the remittances gap filled or it drops toward level null.

Two live pension-policy statuses could not be confirmed and are stated as unresolved rather than asserted: (a) whether the NYC retirement systems' trustees adopted the midstream/downstream private-markets fossil-fuel exclusion proposed in December 2024 for early-2025 presentation, and (b) the outcome of the June 30, 2025 deadline for public-markets asset managers to file compliant net-zero plans. The Comptroller's Bureau of Asset Management can close both.
